preamble: Labialization of the voiced dental fricative [ð] to the voiceless labiodental [f]. It is a defining Sabellic (Osco-Umbrian) innovation: the Proto-Italic word-internal [ð] from PIE *dʰ, which Latin turned into d (medius), appears in Oscan, Umbrian and South Picene as f (Oscan mefiaí 'in the middle'). The change merged the dental with the labial fricative, as initial *θ > f had done earlier across Italic. Some scholars reconstruct the Proto-Italic medial fricative as voiceless *θ, in which case the Sabellic change is θ > f; the f-reflex itself is not in doubt, and Latin borrowed Sabellic rūfus 'red' with its medial f.

examples.to: mefiaí 'in the middle' (loc. sg. f.), mefiú (nom. sg. f.)
examples.note: Latin keeps a dental (d) from the same *ð; Oscan has f.
Latin rūfus, with its non-Latin medial f, is a loan from Sabellic; native Latin has d or b in this root (rōbus, ruber).

sources: de Vaan, M. (2008). Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages. Leiden: Brill. https://brill.com/display/title/12612
